pm14.notes: All points correct and cited. Padded at 212 words: the floating-disc, fibre-development and disc-limit sections were not asked for, and the core answer needs about half the length.
pm14.answer:
Most mills choose disc refiners because they cost less to buy and run, and they are easier to keep in good condition. Smook lists these advantages over conical refiners [DOC 01a335fe-bfba-4f11-b32c-df2de03d8521 p.1]:
- Lower no-load energy use, and the benefit grows as energy costs rise.
- They can run at higher stock consistency.
- They take higher loading and higher rotational speed.
- Plate design is more versatile.
- Wear is self-correcting. High and low spots mate evenly, which conical refiners don't do.
- They have a smaller footprint.
- They cost less capital per ton of production.

The floating-disc design is a further advantage. A rotating disc sits between two stationary plates. Pressure is equal on both faces, so the disc centres itself and the energy splits equally between the two sides. Axial thrust balances, so no thrust bearing is needed [DOC 01a335fe-bfba-4f11-b32c-df2de03d8521 p.1].

Conical refiners do not give better fibre development. At the same operating conditions, conical and disc refiners develop fibres in a similar way [DOC 01a335fe-bfba-4f11-b32c-df2de03d8521 p.1].

Disc refiners do have a limit. Their maximum speed depends on disc diameter, which limits capacity [DOC 01a335fe-bfba-4f11-b32c-df2de03d8521 p.3]. Newer conical designs are not limited by circumferential speed, so they can give lower-intensity action. That suits hardwood furnishes [DOC 01a335fe-bfba-4f11-b32c-df2de03d8521 p.4].

pm13.notes: Accurate and fully cited. It only implies, rather than states, that a good nozzle has a laminar zone. The plugging and inspection-frequency paragraph was not asked for and pushes the answer past 150 words.
pm13.answer:
Look at the water stream. A worn nozzle has a very short laminar zone, and the flow breaks up and disperses as soon as it leaves the orifice. If it does that, replace it [DOC a1b709c1-b90f-4687-ad80-b9fb21515901 p.3].

Exception: some nozzle types never have a laminar zone. Self-purging nozzles are an example. Their orifice is made of two pieces of metal, so the stream breaks up right at the nozzle even when it is new. Don't judge those by this test [DOC a1b709c1-b90f-4687-ad80-b9fb21515901 p.3].

Plugging also shows in the spray pattern, so don't read a distorted pattern as wear without checking. High-hardness water (over 100 ppm CaCO3) can plug nozzles with scale, so the guide says to monitor the spray pattern [DOC a1b709c1-b90f-4687-ad80-b9fb21515901 p.12]. It also says to inspect fan nozzles daily for plugging. At each shutdown, check the spray quality of nozzles you can't see while running [DOC a1b709c1-b90f-4687-ad80-b9fb21515901 p.12].

The library has no source on other visual signs, such as orifice enlargement or a changed fan angle.

pm15.notes: Misreads the question as a weight split and wrongly says the library has no source. Misses the high-yield hot-stock-refined base, the lower-yield well-refined top, and the starch/sizing point. Core claims uncited.
pm15.answer:
The library has no source for a typical base-to-top split in two-ply kraft linerboard. I searched twice and found no basis-weight percentages for the two plies.

From general engineering knowledge, uncited: the base ply is usually about 65–80% of the sheet weight, and the top liner about 20–35%. The base is cheaper, bulkier fiber such as unbleached softwood kraft, sometimes with hardwood or recycled fiber. The top ply is higher-quality, cleaner, brighter fiber for surface, printability and strength. The exact split depends on the mill and the grade.

What the library does say is general and doesn't give a ratio:
- Multi-ply board puts higher-quality grades in the outer plies and lower-quality, bulkier fiber inside. [DOC c93229dc-2711-42b6-9211-821d0e0902e1 p.12]
- A white top liner needs its own fiber-prep system, because the top ply has to be so clean. [DOC c93229dc-2711-42b6-9211-821d0e0902e1 p.9]
- In a 3-ply linerboard trial, virgin kraft went in the outer plies and a recycled/virgin mix in the center. [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.39]

If you want PM1's actual split, I can look for it in the grade or trial reports.

pm16.notes: Does not distinguish SEL (intensity) from specific energy (amount of refining, net kWh/t). Otherwise accurate, the formula is cited to p.41, and the calculation is correct.
pm16.answer:
**Specific edge load (SEL), also called refining intensity, is net refiner power divided by the length of bar edge crossings per second. It is about 1.2 Ws/m for your refiner.**

It is the energy applied per metre of bar crossing, in watt-seconds per metre. A higher SEL gives more fibre cutting and shortening. A lower SEL gives more fibrillation [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.34]. Net power is motor power minus no-load power [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.23].

The formula is SEL = Net kW / (Bar Edge Length × Motor Speed × 1 min / 60 s) [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.41].

Calculation:
- Crossing rate = 30 km/rev × 600 rpm ÷ 60 s/min = 30 × 10 rev/s = 300 km/s
- SEL = 363 kW ÷ 300 km/s = 363,000 W ÷ 300,000 m/s ≈ **1.21 Ws/m**

This matches the AFT manual's worked example, which uses the same inputs and gets 1.2 Ws/m [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.41].

pm17.notes: Misses the key 'why it matters' point: reduced-diameter plates save 30–150 hp (e.g. 46→40 in ≈150 hp). At 289 words it is padded with the intensity formula and the measurement-difficulty discussion.
pm17.answer:
No-load power is mainly set by the rotor diameter and rotational speed. The plate bar and groove pattern and its wear state also matter. Flow, consistency and plate gap have only a minor effect. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.32]

**What drives it**
- Speed: no-load is proportional to rotational speed cubed. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.33]
- Diameter: it scales with active plate diameter to the power of 4.3. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.33]
- Plate pattern: groove depth and the hydraulic section ratio (groove width over bar plus groove width) have a large effect. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.33]
- Plate wear: no-load is highest with new plates and can fall 60–80% when they are fully worn. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.32]
- Rotor mass: it has no effect. Mass only affects start-up acceleration time and torsional loads. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.32]
- Formula: NL (hp) = 102 × (RPM/100)³ × (Da/100)^4.3 × (2Gw/(Bw+Gw)) × (Gd/4). [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.33]

**Why it matters**
- No-load power only pumps and shears the fluid. It does not change the pulp. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.32]
- It must be subtracted from motor load to get the net power applied to the fibers. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.23]
- Refining intensity uses that net power: I = (Applied Motor Power – No-Load) / (RPM × Bar Edge Length × min/60s). A wrong no-load therefore gives a wrong intensity and wrong specific energy. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.23]
- Because no-load drifts as plates wear, the same motor kW does less work on the fiber late in plate life. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.32]
- It is hard to measure accurately, because the rotor can lean on a stator and inflate the reading. Calculated values are often used instead. [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.32]

I did not check PM1 refiner data for this answer.

pm18.notes: Accurate, and the general-knowledge ranking is labelled. Omits RCT's caliper and operator sensitivity, McKee and the ~0.7 mm span. At 267 words it is padded with a conversion factor and box-compression background.
pm18.answer:
**Short answer:** Both tests measure how well a paper strip resists edgewise compression. They differ in how the strip is held. SCT/STFI is generally the better predictor of box performance, but the library has no source that ranks the two directly.

**How they differ**
- **Ring crush (RCT)** is the traditional method. A ½" x 6" strip is rolled into a short cylinder about 2" in diameter. It is then compressed axially between two plates, and the maximum load is recorded [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.18].
- **Short-span compression (STFI/SCT)** is now more widely used [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.18]. It is measured over a very small region so the sample cannot buckle, and failure comes from the fibre wall collapsing [DOC 6e312421-09ec-48b8-97ec-a68bbff246e8 p.23].
- The two give different numbers. In one cross-direction linerboard study, STFI = 1.436 × ring compression [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.57]. The same report says results vary from method to method and are often hard to convert [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.57].

**Box performance**
- Compressive strength is the most important requirement for corrugated boxes. It relates to edgewise compression (ECT), which depends mainly on the liner and the fluting [DOC c93229dc-2711-42b6-9211-821d0e0902e1 p.5].
- Ring crush is considered to relate to the eventual compression strength of the combined board [DOC c93229dc-2711-42b6-9211-821d0e0902e1 p.7].

The library has no source for this; from general engineering knowledge: ring crush can fail by buckling or edge crushing instead of true compressive failure. That makes it less reliable than SCT, particularly on lightweight or high-performance grades. SCT correlates better with ECT and box compression. Neither test captures box-specific effects such as flat crush or converting damage.

ce14.notes: Accurate and fully cited. The closing paragraph on the source's 250-inch example and its rounding, plus the slot-length caveat, are unrequested extras.
ce14.answer:
One Uhle box on a 300-inch machine at 2,500 fpm needs about 4,500–6,000 cfm. This assumes the slot runs the full 300 inches. The real slot length is a bit different, so treat it as an estimate.

- **Slot width:** a total slot width of 1" is required at 2,500 fpm. Slot area depends only on machine speed [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.5].
- **Vacuum factor:** the range is 15–20 cfm per square inch of slot area [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.5].
- **Calculation:** slot area is 300 in × 1 in = 300 in². Airflow is 300 in² × 15–20 cfm/in² = 4,500–6,000 cfm.

The source's own example is a 250" machine at 2,500 fpm, which it gives as 4,000–5,000 cfm per box [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.5]. Applying 15–20 to 250 in² gives 3,750–5,000, so the source's low end looks rounded. That flow sizes the box, piping, separator and vacuum source [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.5].

ce13.answer:
**The flow is about 2.24 ft³/s, or roughly 1,000 gal/min.**

The TAPPI formula for a rectangular weir with end contractions, English units, is Q = 3.33 × (L – 0.2 × H) × H^1.5, with Q in ft³/s and L and H in ft [DOC 2324ca0e-e2cb-4ac4-8f6c-1c90e2a03701 p.4].

Calculation with L = 2 ft and H = 0.5 ft:
- L – 0.2 × H = 2 – 0.1 = 1.9 ft
- H^1.5 = 0.5^1.5 = 0.3536
- Q = 3.33 × 1.9 × 0.3536 ≈ 2.24 ft³/s

The gal/min figure uses 7.48 gal/ft³, which is general knowledge and not from the library: 2.24 × 7.48 × 60 ≈ 1,004 gal/min.

The document says L should be 4 to 8 times H [DOC 2324ca0e-e2cb-4ac4-8f6c-1c90e2a03701 p.4]. Here L/H is exactly 4, so you are at the lower limit of that range.

ce16.notes: Accurate and fully cited, and the answer comes first. The plate-wear note, formula-term explanation and second-source mention are unrequested padding.
ce16.answer:
Calculation: (720/900)³ = 0.8³ = 0.512.

No-load power falls by about 49%, so it drops to roughly 51% of its previous value. The AFT manual says refiner no-load power is proportional to the third power of rotational speed [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.33]. Its formula has the term NL = 102 x (RPM/100)³ x … [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.33]. The other terms are plate diameter, groove width, bar width and groove depth. They stay the same when only speed changes, so they cancel in the ratio. A second source gives the same cubic speed dependence [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.30].

The library gives no absolute no-load figure for your refiner, so I can't give kW or hp. If you tell me the current no-load, multiply it by 0.512. The manual says no-load also falls as plates wear, by as much as 60–80% [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.32]. Use the current plate wear state when you take the baseline.

ce15.notes: Accurate, and the formula is cited to the TAPPI source. The kW conversion, the 75% efficiency example and the note on garbled page text were not asked for and pad the answer.
ce15.answer:
The pump needs about 52.5 hp of hydraulic power, which is about 39 kW.

The TAPPI formula is hydraulic pump power (hp) = Q × H / 1714. Q is flow in gal/min and H is the pump's differential pressure in psi [DOC 2324ca0e-e2cb-4ac4-8f6c-1c90e2a03701 p.3]. The page text is garbled, so I read the 1714 divisor from the formula's layout.

Calculation: 1,500 × 60 / 1714 = 90,000 / 1714 ≈ 52.5 hp.

For kW, I used the 0.746 kW/hp factor [DOC a92ccac2-eca7-4b0a-a2cc-bd07d3da9fa5 p.3]: 52.5 × 0.746 ≈ 39.2 kW.

This is the power delivered to the fluid. The motor shaft power (BHP) is higher by the pump efficiency. I have no efficiency figure for this pump, so I can't give a number. For example, at 75% efficiency the shaft power would be 52.5 / 0.75 = 70 hp. The 75% is only an illustration.

ce17.notes: Gives the laminar limit as about 2,000; the key says about 2,300. Mentions plug flow but omits the plug→mixed→turbulent sequence and the hump/dip in the head-loss curve. Gap is properly labelled. The extra library section pushes it to 229 words.
ce17.answer:
The library has no source for the Reynolds-number criterion. From general engineering knowledge:

- **Deciding laminar or turbulent:** Calculate the Reynolds number, Re = ρvD/μ (equivalently vD/ν). In a round pipe, flow is laminar below about 2,000 and turbulent above about 4,000. Between those values it is transitional. Most mill piping runs far above 4,000.
- **How pulp stock differs:** A fibre suspension is not a simple Newtonian liquid. At low consistency it behaves roughly like water. As consistency rises, the fibres form a network, so the flow is plug-like. A water annulus forms at the wall, and the friction loss curve has its own regimes. Laminar and turbulent regimes then depend on consistency, fibre type and velocity, and a single Re is a poor guide. Medium-consistency stock only flows like a fluid once it is fluidized by turbulence.

What the library does say:
- Stock at 2–6% consistency can be treated as an incompressible fluid with flow properties similar to water. Pumping characteristics up to about 6% are essentially the same as for water [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.34].
- Pipe friction loss differs somewhat with consistency and pulp type [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.34].
- Medium-consistency units fluidize suspensions up to 12% so they behave like Newtonian fluids, which reduces power consumption [DOC 5964733d-306e-4207-a72d-c3ebb900a35e p.17].
- The headbox is meant to create controlled turbulence to prevent fibre flocculation [DOC 66857f06-84b5-470f-ada6-025ffe226134 p.4].

ce18.notes: The answer presents the thermocompressor as part of a cascade, not as an alternative to one. 246 words is well over the target, with unrequested controls and benefits sections. Citations are supported, and the nozzle mechanism is labelled as general knowledge.
ce18.answer:
A thermocompressor is a steam ejector. It uses high-pressure steam to lift low-pressure blow-through steam to a useful intermediate pressure, so the steam can be reused.

- **Principle:** Low-pressure blow-through steam is mixed with high-pressure motive steam and boosted. It is then reused, usually in the same section [DOC 212d6dd4-0711-4fdc-8e33-735d3a13d5de p.12].
- **Internals:** The body has a suction port for the low-pressure steam, a high-pressure steam inlet, a spindle, a nozzle and a diffuser. The discharge is intermediate-pressure steam [DOC 212d6dd4-0711-4fdc-8e33-735d3a13d5de p.12]. In general ejector practice, the motive steam accelerates through the nozzle. This draws in the suction steam, and the diffuser turns the velocity back into pressure. The library does not describe those steps, so that part is from general engineering knowledge.
- **Role in a cascade:** The flow-through and flash steam from one dryer group is used again to heat other dryers, which is a form of heat recovery [DOC f2d6b892-8f3a-49f6-bfb1-8f6beada12e7 p.2]. Condensate drains properly only if steam-side pressure is higher than condensate-side pressure [DOC f2d6b892-8f3a-49f6-bfb1-8f6beada12e7 p.2]. The thermocompressor keeps that differential pressure, for example 0.7 bar on the 3rd dryer group in the explainer's example [DOC f2d6b892-8f3a-49f6-bfb1-8f6beada12e7 p.29].
- **Benefits:** Each section gets independent pressure control, and sections can be grouped freely. It also avoids the loss of electrical generation that would occur if the motive steam were used elsewhere [DOC 212d6dd4-0711-4fdc-8e33-735d3a13d5de p.12].
- **Controls:** The system uses a makeup valve, a low-select switch, and pressure and differential pressure controllers [DOC 212d6dd4-0711-4fdc-8e33-735d3a13d5de p.12].

n09.notes: Accurate, and all four MUST points are fully cited, plus the worked example. At 293 words it is about twice the target, padded with the torque assumption, SEL ignoring fiber characteristics, and too-high/too-low SEL effects.
n09.answer:
**What it is:** Specific edge load (SEL), also called refining intensity, is the energy applied per unit length of bar crossing [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.34]. It describes how hard each bar-edge impact is. It is usually expressed in watt-seconds per meter (Ws/m) [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.23].

**How it's calculated:** SEL is the net power divided by the bar edge length times the speed. Net power is gross power minus no-load power [DOC d9815fa5-40a2-474b-9932-eaf665991fc0 p.29]. The AFT manual gives SEL = Net kW / (Bar Edge Length × Motor Speed × 1 min / 60 s). Its worked example uses 363 kW net, 30 km/rev of bar edge length and 600 rpm, which gives 1.2 Ws/m [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.41]. The theory assumes torque is proportional to normal force, so power tracks the load on the fibers [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.23]. SEL ignores fiber characteristics [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.24].

**Why recycled fiber wants a lower SEL:**
- A higher SEL gives more fiber shortening and cutting. A lower SEL gives more pronounced fibrillation. The deck states plainly that "Recycling requires lower SEL" [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.34].
- In the cited trial on writing and printing papers, the lower SEL curve (500 Ws/km) gave higher tensile and better tear than the 1,500 Ws/km curve at the same energy. The deck's conclusion is "Lower SEL provides better properties" [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.35].
- Recycled fiber has already been shortened and weakened, and it is not stated in the sources why this matters. That is general engineering knowledge, not from the library: recycled fiber has little length to lose, so cutting costs strength.
- Too high an SEL also causes plate clashing, short plate life and poor strength development. Too low an SEL gives inefficient freeness drop and poor fiber development [DOC 856ff3f6-9be4-42e7-b4dc-fee63dfd3cfd p.36].

n10.notes: Accurate and fully cited. The answer leads with $18,000. The seal-water note and the 86% document example were not asked for and add length.
n10.answer:
About $18,000 a year is wasted, which is 30% of the $60,000.

The TAPPI method is $Ew = $E × (1 − %OC) [DOC a92ccac2-eca7-4b0a-a2cc-bd07d3da9fa5 p.4]. Here that is $60,000 × (1 − 0.70) = $18,000.

The method assumes a worn pump keeps drawing the same power and seal water as a new one. It just moves less air [DOC a92ccac2-eca7-4b0a-a2cc-bd07d3da9fa5 p.3]. The document's own example is an 86% pump that wastes 14% of its power [DOC a92ccac2-eca7-4b0a-a2cc-bd07d3da9fa5 p.3].

The same factor applies to seal water cost, so about 30% of that is wasted too [DOC a92ccac2-eca7-4b0a-a2cc-bd07d3da9fa5 p.4].

The 70% figure is only valid if the test was done at the pump's optimum vacuum level. It must also be compared with the manufacturer's curve at the actual rpm [DOC a92ccac2-eca7-4b0a-a2cc-bd07d3da9fa5 p.3].

n11.notes: Omits that fibre modulus and strength limit ultimate strength in well-bonded sheets, insensitivity to pulping yield at constant density, and CD needs with orientation/drying-strain effects. Extra refining and Z-strength bullets push length.
n11.answer:
Density and fibre stiffness mainly control it. Wet pressing and freeness (refining) are the main machine levers on density.

- The Institute of Paper Chemistry survey lists wet pressing first and freeness second as the significant papermaking factors for compressive strength [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.20].
- The same report says that higher density increases the compressive strength of linerboard and medium [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.41]. It adds that densification by press drying raises compressive strength and that high density promotes fibre-to-fibre bonding [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.29].
- Fibre stiffness matters too. A figure in the report relates STFI compressive strength to fibre modulus at a fixed density of 700 kg/m³ [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.13]. Stiff hardwood fibres can reach high compressive strengths if the density is high enough [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.29].
- Refining raises compressive strength in a nearly linear relationship to density [DOC 573e2f9c-afca-42a5-b4a6-10980694ab2e p.18].
- Z-direction bond strength also raises compressive strength, rapidly at first and then only up to a certain level of bonding [DOC 168553e0-baa3-4e06-827d-54415678796a p.20].

n12.notes: All points covered and cited. At 195 words it runs over the 150-word target, with extra items from a second document (vacuum couch roll, excess vacuum). It never says outright that fewer boxes, less slot area and higher vacuum dewater better.
n12.answer:
A flatbox near the couch doesn't need more than five or six slots, and the slot widths usually get narrower as the sheet approaches the couch [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.4]. That comes from a general best-practice paper. The library has no PM1-specific flatbox count.

Other ways to reduce table drive load:
- **Remove unneeded flatboxes and boxes with too much slot area.** The paper says there are often too many of both [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.4].
- **Rework the flatbox covers with low-drag ceramics such as silicon nitride.** This can easily save 10–20% of the power across the couch, wire turning roll and other former drives [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.4].
- **Move the high vacuum to near the wet/dry line, after formation is complete.** Pair that with fewer boxes and less slot area [DOC 56ec08f5-d829-4786-b810-b1a7de9c7f74 p.4].
- **Use a vacuum couch roll for part of the dewatering.** Because the couch roll rotates with the fabric, it avoids the high frictional drag of high-vacuum flatboxes [DOC 7d704e0a-0ca7-4284-8fb9-dc6721c03b8a p.12].
- **Avoid excess vacuum.** Extra vacuum wastes pumping energy, wears the forming fabric and increases the power needed to overcome friction between the fabric and the flatbox covers [DOC 7d704e0a-0ca7-4284-8fb9-dc6721c03b8a p.52].
